principles.text: Bet on the founder, not the idea: judge whether the person will succeed, not whether the idea will.
Ask what happens if it works, not what could go wrong; outlandish ideas nobody believes in return the most.
Run fundraising as a full-time sales funnel: about 150 qualified investor targets, repeated follow-ups, a few term sheets.
Venture money is jet fuel; take it only to build something big and fast, otherwise grow off revenue.
You can fake a pitch but not a great product or delighted customers, so talk to customers.

sampleQA.question: How should I run my seed round?

answer.text: Make fundraising a full-time job for one co-founder and run it like a qualified sales funnel.
Target about 150 carefully selected seed funds; expect roughly 50 meetings, 15 second meetings and two term sheets.
Keep the cold email a short trailer with a Loom demo, and follow up two or three times.
Practice on lower-priority investors first, then pitch your dream investors in weeks two or three.

sampleQA.question: Should I raise venture money at all?

answer.text: Only if you want to build something big and fast. VC is jet fuel, and you don't put rocket fuel on a Vespa.
VCs look for 20-50x and angels for 100x, so lifestyle outcomes don't qualify.
Bootstrapping to product-market fit or revenue gives you more investor options and better terms; pre-selling to customers is a good hack.
Never pay to pitch angels or pay a consultant to raise for you.

sampleQA.question: We have six months of cash in a downturn. What now?

answer.text: Aim for 18 months of runway; with six months you will probably die if you don't act.
Make the cuts and extend runway before you pitch investors, and show raw numbers without spin.
Revenue is revenue: take services or consulting work even at lower margin.
Don't use venture debt to extend runway.
